cards.text: This is a psalm of David, written for the choirmaster, so it's made to be sung. A whole group is praying over one person facing a day of trouble, and they start by asking the LORD to answer. It's like the group chat flooding you with prayer hands before your big day, except this group chat has a CHOIR.

cards.question: Then they call on the name of the God of Jacob, the man God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28). What do they ask that name to do for the person in trouble?
Next the group prays about where this person's help will come from: May He send you help from the ___

cards.text: They ask God to sustain this person from Zion, too. Then they bring up this person's gifts and burnt offerings.

cards.question: What does the group ask the LORD to do with this person's gifts?

cards.text: Then a Selah lands right there in the song, and after it the prayers get BIG. They ask God to give this person the desires of their heart.

cards.question: The group has asked God to give this person their heart's desires. What do they pray for this person's plans?
The group pictures the day this person wins. True or false: they plan to keep it quiet.

cards.text: They'll shout for joy and raise a banner in the name of their God, like a whole stadium waving one giant flag. And they ask the LORD to grant every request this person makes.

cards.question: Up to now, the psalm has been one 'may' after another. Then one voice says, 'Now I know.' What changed for him?

answers.text: He's going to wait and see

cards.text: He's sure the LORD saves His anointed and answers him from His holy heaven with the saving power of His right hand. Friend, MY right hand is half a mustache, and HIS right hand SAVES.
Then comes the big comparison: some trust in chariots, and others in horses. I trusted my sharp edges once, and those got me a one-way trip to the back of a junk drawer.

cards.question: The group praying in this psalm doesn't trust in chariots or horses: we trust in the ___ of the LORD our God.
The ones who trust in chariots and horses collapse and fall. What happens to the ones who trust in the name of the LORD?

answers.text: They rise up and stand firm

cards.question: The last line finally names the person this whole psalm has been praying for. Who is it?

cards.text: Then they ask the LORD to answer them on the day they call. The song opened asking Him to answer, and it closes on that same ask.

findings.problem: This fill in the blank asks the baker to finish the wording of the line ('May He send you help from the ___'). The word 'sanctuary' hasn't appeared on any earlier card, so the baker is guessing the psalm's wording, not reasoning out its meaning. Ask about the picture instead, such as where help comes from, set up on a story card.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: Multiple choice dominates the stop. Six of the nine choice cards are multiple choice, two are fill in the blank and only one is true or false.

rule.text: No stop repeats another stop's pattern, and no type dominates a stop by a wide margin.

findings.problem: The card is two flat lines of summary with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a list of verse contents, not a storyteller carrying the moment.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The second half of 20:3, the prayer that the LORD 'look favorably on your burnt offerings', is never told. Card 4 only says the group 'bring up' the burnt offerings, and card 5 asks only about the gifts.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: Verse 5 is a wish ('May we shout for joy... and raise a banner'). The card turns it into a flat statement of what will happen ('They'll shout for joy and raise a banner'). Card 8's 'they plan to keep it quiet' has the same drift. Keep it as a prayer, for example 'They pray they'll get to shout for joy...'

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The joke adds to the backstory and doesn't match it. In papa-dorin.md, his edges went soft and worn, and that is why he was replaced and put in the drawer. Nothing says he 'trusted' his sharp edges, and sharp edges didn't send him to the drawer. Their wearing out did. The comparison doesn't click instantly.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: 'It closes on that same ask' overstates the match. Verse 1 asks the LORD to answer 'you in the day of trouble', and verse 9 asks Him to 'Answer us on the day we call'. The two asks are alike, but they aren't the same. Say something like 'it closes asking Him to answer again.'

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true. "Same words" means an exact match.
